> agent (Claude Opus) with live WebSearch/WebFetch. Citations are leads the
> agent grounded at fetch time, not re-verified individually by the
> coordinator; the items that materially shaped the proposals (RuboCop
> Safe/SafeAutoCorrect, ESLint 10-pass fix loop, Getafix specificity,

# Prior Art for Improving Auto-Generated Auto-Fix Rules (Credence)

Research report on techniques to raise the **precision, generality, safety, and non-redundancy**
of auto-generated Elixir auto-fix rules. Credence's shape: AST pattern-match rules with source
patches, every rule must auto-fix, validated by a corpus findings snapshot ratchet, generated by an LLM
harness (weak model → clumsy solution → classifier extracts before/after anti-pattern → novelty
check → equivalence check → agent implements rule+tests → gate: new-test + mutation + suite +
corpus).

Sources are linked inline. Each item gives a technique summary followed by the concrete
transferable idea for Credence (marked **→**).

---

## A. Learning / synthesizing program-transformation rules from examples

The dominant lesson across this literature: **generalize only what actually varies, keep the
invariant context, and require statistical support before promoting a pattern to a rule.**

### Getafix (Meta/Facebook, OOPSLA 2019)
Getafix mines past human fixes for a bug category, computes AST edits, then combines
**anti-unification** (generalize two edits into a pattern with typed "holes" where they differ)
with **hierarchical clustering** (a dendrogram: leaves are concrete edits, higher nodes are more
abstract anti-unified patterns). Crucially it retains the *surrounding unchanged code* in the
pattern as context, which is what stops over-generalization — it learns "add null check before
*this* call shape," not just "add null check." At suggestion time it ranks candidate patterns by
**specificity** (a more specific pattern matches in fewer places and is preferred), then validates
that the produced patch compiles and clears the original warning. It predicted the exact
human-written fix as the top suggestion between **12% and 91%** depending on bug category.
- Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.06111 · https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3360585
- Blog: https://engineering.fb.com/2018/11/06/developer-tools/getafix-how-facebook-tools-learn-to-fix-bugs-automatically/

**→** Two directly usable ideas: (1) make each generated rule's LHS carry *invariant context nodes*
(not just the changed subtree) so it fires narrowly; (2) when the harness has several candidate
generalizations, rank by specificity — prefer the pattern that matches fewest corpus locations
while still covering the training example, and treat "matches a huge fraction of the corpus" as a
smell for over-generality.

### Refazer (Rolim et al., ICSE 2017)
Refazer synthesizes AST-level program transformations from before/after edit examples using
Microsoft's **PROSE** inductive-synthesis engine, defining a DSL of edit operators and searching for
the simplest program consistent with all examples. On student assignment fixes it repaired 87% of
students; on repetitive developer edits in three C# projects it learned the intended transformation
in **84%** of 56 scenarios from only **2.9 examples on average**.
- Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.09000 · https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~bjoern/papers/rolim-refazer-icse2017.pdf

**→** Multiple examples sharpen a rule fast. Rather than generalizing from the single (clumsy
solution, gold solution) diff, the harness could cluster *several* weak-model failures that share a
transformation and synthesize the rule from the whole cluster — the intersection of examples
automatically removes accidental specifics and yields a tighter, better-supported LHS.

### Revisar (Rolim et al., 2018)
Revisar mines commit histories: it computes AST diffs via **tree edit distance**, clusters edits
that share a pattern, and — when possible — compiles each pattern to an executable **Refaster**
before/after template (the Error Prone rule language). It only reports a pattern as "useful" when it
recurs across **≥3 projects**, discovering 89 patterns of which 64% were absent from existing tools.
- Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.03806 · Site: https://sites.google.com/view/revisar/home

**→** A cross-source support threshold is a cheap generality filter. Credence's corpus can play the
role Revisar's "≥3 projects" plays: only accept a generated rule if the *bad* pattern occurs in
multiple independent corpus files (evidence it's a real recurring anti-pattern, not a one-off from
one weak-model quirk).

### Phoenix (Bavishi et al., FSE 2019)
Phoenix does data-driven synthesis of repairs for static-analysis violations in three stages —
collect violation-fixing patches, learn repair strategies, suggest repairs — using **GumTree** for
AST differencing and Eclipse JDT to manipulate ASTs. It generalizes concrete patches into
parameterized repair strategies keyed to the analyzer's warning.
- Paper: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3338906.3338952 · PDF: https://rbavishi.github.io/docs/fse19-phoenix.pdf

**→** Confirms the pipeline shape Credence already uses (diff → generalize → synthesize →
validate); the reusable detail is anchoring each learned strategy to a *named trigger* so rules stay
scoped to the situation they were learned for.

### GenPat / InferRule / PyEvolve — transformation-by-example (TBE)
GenPat (ASE 2019) infers a reusable transformation from a **single** example by mining "big code"
statistics to decide which parts to generalize vs keep concrete. The TBE line formalizes a rule as
two components: a **Rule** (the edit) and a **Guard** (a validation predicate that decides where the
rule may apply). PyEvolve uses InferRule as its synthesizer; recent work fuses LLMs with TBE.
- GenPat: https://xgdsmileboy.github.io/files/paper/genpat-ase19.pdf
- LLM+TBE: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.07138

**→** Adopt the explicit **Rule + Guard** split. Each Credence rule should carry a separately
testable guard predicate (structural preconditions: arity, literal-ness, that a variable is unused,
that no macro/DSL context surrounds it) distinct from the rewrite. Guards are where precision lives
and are individually mutation-testable.

### Uber Piranha / PolyglotPiranha
A structural find-and-replace (rewrite) engine plus a library of language-specific **cleanup rules**
(simplify boolean expressions, collapse constant `if`, delete empty declarations, inline
single-use locals). Its distinctive mechanism is **rule chaining/cascade**: applying one rewrite
triggers dependent cleanup rules until a fixpoint, so a single seed edit propagates a full,
consistent cleanup. Used in production to remove ~2000 stale feature flags.
- Blog: https://www.uber.com/blog/piranha/ · Repo: https://github.com/uber/piranha · Polyglot: https://github.com/uber/piranha/blob/master/POLYGLOT_README.md · Paper: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9276556/

**→** A small, curated library of *general* cleanup rules (dead-code removal, boolean/`if`
simplification, redundant-binding inlining) composes with domain rules and is safer per-rule than
bespoke multi-step patches. Credence could keep such primitives as trusted building blocks that
generated rules emit into, rather than re-synthesizing structural cleanup each time.

### comby, ast-grep, Semgrep autofix — the pattern+rewrite substrate
All three express a rule as a **match template** and a **rewrite template** sharing metavariables,
so the fix reuses captured code verbatim. comby is parser-combinator based and comment/string-aware
across ~every language (https://comby.dev, https://arxiv.org/pdf/... PLDI'24
https://danieltrt.github.io/papers/pldi24.pdf). ast-grep is Tree-sitter based with `$META` vars, a
`fix:` key, and a **FixConfig** that can expand the rewrite range (`expandStart`/`expandEnd`) until a
boundary rule stops matching (https://ast-grep.github.io/guide/rewrite-code.html). Semgrep's `fix:`
key substitutes metavariables and **ellipsis metavariables** (`$...ARGS`) so an unknown-arity
argument list is preserved through the rewrite, plus `focus-metavariable` and `fix-regex` with a
`count` (https://semgrep.dev/docs/writing-rules/autofix).

**→** Ellipsis/spread metavariables and range-expansion are the features that keep a rewrite from
mangling the parts it shouldn't touch. Ensure Credence's patch representation can capture-and-replay
"the rest of the arguments / the body unchanged" as a first-class hole, so patches never have to
reconstruct untouched code (a common over-fire source).

### OpenRewrite recipes (Moderne)
Recipes traverse a **Lossless Semantic Tree (LST)** — a *type-attributed* and *format-preserving*
model — with the visitor pattern, matching a target by its **resolved type** and editing precisely,
so the same recipe is deterministic and re-runnable. Recipes are authored three ways: declarative
YAML composition, a compiler-checked **Refaster** before/after template, or an imperative visitor for
hard cases. The pitch is explicitly "no regex guesswork, no LLM nondeterminism, no regressions on
re-run."
- Docs: https://docs.openrewrite.org/ · LST: https://docs.openrewrite.org/concepts-and-explanations/lossless-semantic-trees · Recipes: https://docs.openrewrite.org/concepts-and-explanations/recipes

**→** Type/binding resolution eliminates whole classes of false matches that pure AST-shape matching
suffers. Where Elixir permits (e.g., resolving that a call is `Enum.map/2` vs a local `map`, or that
a name is a module alias), let generated guards consult binding/alias info rather than bare syntax —
and keep patches format-preserving so re-running is a no-op fixpoint.

### Sorald (Etemadi et al., TDSC 2022) and SpongeBugs (Marcilio et al., JSS 2020)
Both are **template/metaprogramming** repair systems for SonarQube/SpotBugs Java rules. Sorald fixes
**65% (852/1307)** of violations *that meet its repair preconditions* — the key phrase: it only fires
where structural preconditions guarantee a safe fix (https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.12033,
https://github.com/ASSERT-KTH/sorald). SpongeBugs covers 11 widely used rules, submitted 946 fixes as
real PRs, and reports **<0.6% false positives** with templates that can emit multi-line patches
(https://dvmarcilio.github.io/papers/jss20-spongebugs.pdf).

**→** "Repair preconditions" is the operational form of a safety gate: for each rule, define the
precise structural precondition under which the fix is provably safe, and *decline to fire otherwise*
(no fix beats a wrong fix). SpongeBugs' sub-1% false-positive bar is a concrete precision target to
hold generated rules to on the corpus.

---

## B. Validating auto-fixes and rewrite rules

### Alive2 — bounded translation validation (Lopes et al., PLDI 2021)
Alive2 takes pre- and post-transformation LLVM IR and asks an SMT solver (Z3) whether the output
**refines** the input: for every input on which the source is defined, the target produces the same
result and introduces no new undefined behavior. It is *bounded* (loops unrolled to a limit) so it
can miss bugs, but it is designed to **never raise false alarms**; running it over LLVM's test suite
found 47 new bugs and forced 8 clarifications to the IR spec.
- Paper: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3453483.3454030 · Repo: https://github.com/AliveToolkit/alive2

**→** Two transferable ideas: (1) Alive2's refinement model is not Credence's fix contract:
a Credence fix must give exactly the same answer for every admitted input. Any rewrite that changes
undefined or edge behavior must first narrow its guard so those inputs are not admitted, with that
safety assumption declared and tested. (2) Prefer a checker that is sound-for-rejection (no false
"equivalent") even if incomplete (may say "unknown"), matching Credence's corpus-ratchet posture.

### SafeRefactor / JDolly (Soares & Gheyi et al., SBES 2009, TSE 2012)
SafeRefactor checks a refactoring is behavior-preserving by **auto-generating a test suite** (Randoop)
over the methods common to both versions and diffing behavior; JDolly *exhaustively generates* small
programs as inputs. Their differential-testing method specifically hunts **overly strong or overly
weak preconditions** in refactoring engines, and across 153,444 transformations of Eclipse/NetBeans/
JastAdd it found 63 behavioral-change bugs.
- SafeRefactor: https://www.dsc.ufcg.edu.br/~spg/uploads/sbes09.pdf · TSE: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/tse12.pdf

**→** Their "find overly-strong/weak preconditions by differential testing" is exactly a **guard
tuning loop**: generate many small programs that a rule's guard accepts, run before/after, and any
behavioral divergence pinpoints a too-weak guard (over-fire); any accepted-but-unfixed case pinpoints
a too-strong guard (missed generality). This is a ready-made way to auto-tighten generated guards.

### Differential fuzzing of LLM refactorings (2026)
This study checks functional equivalence of LLM refactorings with **Eq@DFuzz**: no predefined
tests — it fuzzes 1000–2000 diverse inputs (Atheris), runs both versions, and calls them equivalent
only if outputs match on **all** inputs. Across 3,538 refactorings from six models, **19–35% were
functionally non-equivalent** (GPT-4o best at 18.6%, Codestral worst at ~35%), and — the headline
warning — **~21% of the non-equivalent refactorings still passed the existing test suite.**
- Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15761 · HTML: https://arxiv.org/html/2602.15761v1

**→** Strong empirical mandate for Credence's equivalence check: passing the project's tests does
**not** imply equivalence. Back the LLM equivalence classifier with an executable differential check —
generate inputs (StreamData), run before/after, require identical observable behavior — before any
behavior-changing rewrite is accepted. Budget for the fact that even good models emit ~20% semantics-
altering "refactorings."

### Property-based testing with StreamData (Elixir)
StreamData is Elixir's native QuickCheck-style library: the `check all` macro draws generated inputs
and **shrinks** counterexamples to minimal failing cases. It is the idiomatic vehicle for an
equivalence property `before(x) == after(x)` in Credence's own language.
- Blog: https://elixir-lang.org/blog/2017/10/31/stream-data-property-based-testing-and-data-generation-for-elixir/ · Repo: https://github.com/whatyouhide/stream_data

**→** For rules whose before/after are both executable (pure transformations of a value/expression),
auto-emit a StreamData equivalence property as part of the generated test set; shrinking hands the
harness a minimal over-fire witness it can feed back into guard refinement.

### Mutation testing applied to rules (Petrovic & Ivankovic, Google, ICSE 2021)
Mutation testing injects small faults (mutants) and measures the fraction the test suite kills;
Google runs it inside code review at scale and found it meaningfully drives test improvements.
- Paper: https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~rjust/publ/mutation_testing_practices_icse_2021.pdf

**→** Credence already gates on a mutation check; the refinement is *what* to mutate — mutate the
**guard/LHS** (drop a context node, loosen an arity constraint, flip a literal check) and require an
existing test to fail. A rule whose guard mutants survive is under-tested and probably over-general;
this is a direct precision signal, not just a coverage signal.

### ESLint: fixable vs. suggestion (safe-autofix policy)
ESLint splits remediations in two. A **fix** (`meta.fixable`) is applied automatically by `--fix` and
must be safe and mechanical — no logic change. A **suggestion** (`meta.hasSuggestions`) may alter
behavior, is **editor-only / opt-in**, must be a single focused change, and does **not** participate
in multi-pass fixing. The stated decision rule: "if obviously safe and mechanical, autofix; if it
could alter behavior, depends on intent, or has multiple valid outcomes, make it a suggestion."
- Docs: https://eslint.org/docs/latest/extend/custom-rules

**→** Credence mandates auto-fix for every rule, so this is the boundary of what should become a rule
at all: a candidate whose fix "depends on intent or has multiple valid outcomes" should be **rejected
by the gate**, not shipped as a shaky auto-fix. Encode ESLint's decision rule as an acceptance
predicate in the classifier/equivalence stage.

### RuboCop: Safe vs. SafeAutoCorrect taxonomy (highly relevant)
RuboCop separates **two** safety axes. `Safe` = the cop won't produce false positives by design
(the diagnostic is trustworthy). `SafeAutoCorrect` = the automatic fix preserves semantics. They are
independent: `FrozenStringLiteral` is `Safe: true` (the magic comment really is missing) but its
autocorrect is **unsafe** because some literals then need a `+` to avoid being frozen. An unsafe cop
implies an unsafe autocorrect. `-a` applies only safe corrections, `-A` applies everything, `-x`
applies layout-only; every cop's safety is annotated in the default config, and docs insist users
"always review the diff and run the test suite after `-A`."
- Docs: https://docs.rubocop.org/rubocop/latest/usage/autocorrect.html · Rationale: https://metaredux.com/posts/2018/10/27/a-safer-rubocop.html · https://metaredux.com/posts/2020/07/07/a-safer-rubocop-part-deux.html

**→** Adopt the **two-axis safety label** explicitly on every generated rule: *detection-safe* (LHS
never over-fires — the corpus gate proves this) and *correction-safe* (the RHS preserves behavior —
the equivalence check proves this). They are different gates and should be recorded separately; a
rule can pass detection but fail correction (RuboCop's exact `FrozenStringLiteral` situation), and
that combination should route to "reject" under a mandatory-autofix policy.

### clang-tidy fix-it reliability
clang-tidy refuses to apply fixes whose source ranges **overlap**, with one exception: if one fix is
fully contained in another, the larger one wins. Identical warnings are de-duplicated. Fixes inside
macro bodies / template definitions are flagged as dangerous because one expansion's safe edit breaks
another. Fixes attached to *notes* are **off by default** (lower confidence).
- Docs: https://releases.llvm.org/3.9.0/tools/clang/tools/extra/docs/clang-tidy/index.html · Overlap fix: https://reviews.llvm.org/D13516

**→** Concrete conflict-resolution rules to reuse: (1) reject/skip a patch when two rules' edit ranges
overlap (containment excepted); (2) treat edits that land inside **macro expansions** — the Elixir
analogue being `use`/`import`-injected code, `~` sigils, and quoted `defmacro` bodies — as low-
confidence and default them off, mirroring the "fixes-in-notes off by default" stance.

---

## C. LLM-driven rule / linter generation (2023–2026)

### CodeQL query generation with LLMs; Merlin's self-test loop
A recent trend keeps CodeQL as a symbolic backend and uses LLMs to draft/refine queries: CQLLM
(https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/16/1/517) and QLPro (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23644) generate
project-specific scanning rules. **Merlin** is the most transferable: it uses retrieval-augmented
*iterative* CodeQL generation plus a **self-test/debugging mechanism that runs "assistive queries"
generating concrete witnesses** for semantic flaws in a candidate query. A recurring failure across
all systems is hallucinated **deprecated syntax and non-existent modules**.
- Multi-agent CodeQL evolution: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/403441399

**→** Have the harness generate the rule *and* an assistive query/probe that surfaces a **concrete
witness** — a specific corpus snippet the new rule fires on — and force the implementing agent to
inspect that witness before finalizing. Grounding on concrete matches (not just the abstract pattern)
is what catches over-generality and hallucinated matchers early.

### Semgrep Assistant — precision data and how they got it
Semgrep Assistant auto-writes rules and auto-triages findings. It reaches **>95% accuracy** at
labeling findings as false positives and **agrees with human security researchers 96%** of the time
on true positives — but note it is **deliberately tuned to minimize false negatives**, so its FP-side
agreement is only ~41%. The precision came from: (1) rich context (rule metadata, prior triage
decisions on that rule, curated positive/negative examples, and persistent **Assistant Memories**);
(2) prompt framing ("what would a human triaging this consider?"); (3) a **model bake-off with
promptfoo against a 2,000+ finding gold benchmark**; (4) memory, which lifted FPs filtered from
18 → 588 in one study.
- 96% blog: https://semgrep.dev/blog/2025/building-an-appsec-ai-that-security-researchers-agree-with-96-of-the-time/
- Metrics/methodology: https://semgrep.dev/docs/semgrep-assistant/metrics
- Memory: https://semgrep.dev/blog/2025/making-zero-false-positive-sast-a-reality-with-ai-powered-memory/

**→** Three moves: (1) build a **held-out gold benchmark of accept/reject rule decisions** and run a
prompt/model bake-off (promptfoo-style) against it, rather than trusting one prompt; (2) feed the
classifier **prior accept/reject decisions and curated positive/negative corpus snippets** as
context (a "memory") so it stops re-proposing near-duplicates; (3) pick the operating point
deliberately — Credence's zero-over-fire posture is the *opposite* of Semgrep's (minimize false
*positives*/over-fires even at the cost of missing some rules), and the gate thresholds should be set
to that asymmetry on purpose.

### Self-Refine / Reflexion vs. the self-correction ceiling
Self-Refine (https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651) and Reflexion (https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366) show
an LLM can generate → critique → refine its own output and improve on code tasks. **But** Huang et
al. (DeepMind, ICLR 2024, "LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet") show that *intrinsic* self-
correction — no external oracle — often **degrades** quality; the gains in prior work came almost
entirely from access to a ground-truth oracle.
- Self-Refine: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651 · Reflexion: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366
- Cannot self-correct: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798

**→** This validates Credence's architecture and warns against a naive critique loop: the refine loop
**must be closed over an external signal** (the gold reference, corpus over-fire count, mutation
survivors, executable equivalence result), not the model's own opinion. Feed the *actual* corpus/
test/mutation failures back into each refinement iteration; do not let the agent "self-approve."

### LLM-as-judge reliability for code equivalence
Surveys and benchmarks report LLM judges land around **89–94%** accuracy on semantic-correctness
judgments, with completion reliability (ECR@1) ranging 85–100% across models — and a specific,
dangerous failure mode: when shown **semantically equivalent** code, judges frequently **flip to
"wrong,"** anchoring on literal/textual differences instead of intent.
- LLM-as-Judge for SWE survey: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.24367
- Coverage-judge reliability: https://arxiv.org/html/2512.01232

**→** Do not let a single LLM equivalence judgment gate a rewrite. Mitigate the known "flip on
equivalent code" failure by (1) giving the judge explicit equivalence rules (commutativity, dead-
binding elimination, alias-equality) and worked examples; (2) ensembling / self-consistency voting;
and (3) preferring the *executable* differential/property check (Section B) as the authority, with
the LLM judge as a cheap pre-filter only.

### LLM rewrite rules validated by fuzzing/property testing
The differential-fuzzing study (Section B, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15761) is itself the primary
example of validating LLM-produced rewrites by fuzzing; Kaizen (metamorphic fuzzing + differential
testing, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.04058) and RustAssure (differential symbolic testing,
https://arxiv.org/html/2510.07604v1) generalize the pattern to translation/transpilation.

**→** Metamorphic relations are a cheap equivalence oracle when a full spec is absent: "a semantics-
preserving rewrite must not change output for any input." Encode each generated rule's intended
invariant as a metamorphic relation and fuzz it — the harness gets an equivalence verdict without
needing a hand-written test oracle.

---

## D. Rule-set hygiene at scale

### ESLint multi-pass fix loop and conflict resolution
`Linter.verifyAndFix` runs up to **`MAX_AUTOFIX_PASSES = 10`** passes. Within a pass, all fixes are
sorted by descending source range and applied; if two fixes **overlap, only the first is applied**
and the rest wait for the next pass. Across passes it re-runs until stable, and it **detects circular
fixes by comparing the current output to the output two passes ago** (rule A adds a comma, rule B
removes it), halting with a warning instead of looping forever.
- Circular-fix docs: https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/troubleshooting/circular-fixes
- 10-pass discussion: https://github.com/eslint/eslint/issues/17609 · Detection commit: https://github.com/eslint/eslint/pull/19236

**→** If Credence applies multiple rules in one run it needs the same machinery: a **fixpoint loop
with a hard pass cap**, **overlap-based conflict skipping** (first-wins within a pass), and
**cycle detection by output hashing** (compare to N-passes-ago). A generated rule that induces a
cycle with an existing rule is a *rule-interaction defect the gate should catch* by running the whole
ruleset to fixpoint on the corpus, not just the new rule in isolation.

### RuboCop autocorrect loop + infinite-loop / clobbering detection
RuboCop re-runs cops until the source stabilizes and **raises an "Infinite loop detected" error** when
a file's corrected output repeats, catching pairs of cops that undo each other. Its rewriter
(`Parser::Source::TreeRewriter`) raises **"detected clobbering"** when two corrections touch
overlapping ranges. Many real issues trace to two style cops fighting over the same span.
- Infinite loop example: https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/issues/8618 · Clobbering: https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/issues/10375

**→** Same lesson as ESLint from the other major auto-fixer: build **loop detection and overlap
("clobbering") detection into the corpus run**, and treat any new rule that triggers either as a
regression against the existing rule set. This is how you keep a *growing* auto-generated rule set
from silently destabilizing.

### Rule redundancy and subsumption theory
Formally, a rule is **redundant** if removing it doesn't change the system's semantics, and **subsumed**
by another if every application of the first can be replaced by an application of the second with the
same effect (Ehrig et al., "Redundancy and Subsumption in High-Level Replacement Systems").
Tooling that manages rule sets classifies pairs as duplicate / subsuming / overlapping / conflicting.
- Theory: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-46464-8_15

**→** Sharpen the novelty check from "is this pattern textually new?" to a **subsumption test**:
does an existing rule already fire on (and fix) every corpus location the candidate does? If yes, the
candidate is redundant/subsumed — reject. If it fires on a strict superset, it may *replace* the
narrower rule. Computing this over the corpus (which locations each rule matches) makes subsumption
decidable empirically without a theorem prover.

### Benchmarking rule precision on corpora
- **Clippy lintcheck**: builds and runs Clippy on a fixed set of crates (buildable from the most-
  downloaded crates.io crates), logs all warnings, and you **`git diff` the log** to see exactly what
  a new/changed lint does to real code; `--fix` flags suggestions that fail to apply, auto-surfacing
  bad fixes. https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-clippy/blob/master/lintcheck/README.md
- **RuboCop real-world regression**: runs cops (across many generated `EnforcedStyle` configs) against
  real GitHub Ruby to catch false positives/negatives **and crashes**, because unit tests "cover only
  a few code styles" while real code has many. https://speakerdeck.com/pocke/regression-testing-for-rubocop · https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/issues/6805

**→** Credence's zero-over-fire corpus is exactly this discipline; two upgrades from the mature tools:
(1) store the corpus match/fix **log as a checked-in artifact and diff it per rule change**, so every
rule's blast radius is reviewable (Clippy's model); (2) fuzz **rule configuration/parameters**, not
just inputs, and assert **no crashes** on the whole corpus, not only "no over-fire" (RuboCop's model).

### Telemetry-driven tuning — Google Tricorder (Sadowski et al., ICSE 2015)
Tricorder is Google's analysis platform built on a hard empirical rule: **developer trust collapses
above ~10% false positives**, so any analyzer surfaced in review must stay under that bar, measured
by live feedback — a **"Not useful"** button vs. **"Please Fix"** actions (≈93K findings/day drew ~716
Please-Fix vs. ~48 Not-Useful clicks). Noisy analyzers are put on **probation** and disabled if not
fixed.
- Paper: https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/43322.pdf · SWE-book ch.20: https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch20.html

**→** Bake a **quantitative precision bar** into the gate (Tricorder's <10% FP is the canonical
number; SpongeBugs shipped <0.6% for auto-fixes, a better target for silent auto-correction) and, once
rules are in the field, **collect accept/revert telemetry per rule** and auto-demote (probation) any
generated rule whose fixes get reverted often. Precision is not a one-time gate; it's a maintained
signal.

---

## Top 10 transferable ideas, ranked by expected impact for Credence

1. **Executable equivalence, not test-passage, for the equivalence check.** LLM "refactorings" are
   19–35% behavior-changing and ~21% of those still pass existing tests (arxiv 2602.15761). Back the
   LLM equivalence classifier with a StreamData/differential-fuzz property (`before(x) == after(x)`)
   over generated inputs. Highest-leverage safety fix; directly attacks silent over-fixes.

2. **Two-axis safety labels on every rule (RuboCop model): detection-safe vs. correction-safe.**
   Prove LHS-never-over-fires (corpus) and RHS-preserves-behavior (equivalence) as *separate* gates;
   a rule can pass one and fail the other (RuboCop's `FrozenStringLiteral`), and under mandatory
   auto-fix that combination must reject. Cleanly organizes the whole gate.

3. **Rule = Rule + Guard, with the guard as the precision surface (TBE model).** Give each rule an
   explicit, separately-testable guard predicate (arity, literal-ness, unused-binding, no macro/DSL
   context) distinct from the rewrite. Guards are where over-fires are prevented and are individually
   mutation-testable.

4. **Keep invariant context in the LHS and rank candidate generalizations by specificity (Getafix).**
   Have the classifier emit patterns that include surrounding unchanged nodes, and prefer the
   generalization that matches the *fewest* corpus locations while still covering the training
   example. Turns "over-general" from a vibe into a measurable corpus-match count.

5. **Redefine novelty as empirical subsumption over the corpus.** Reject a candidate if an existing
   rule already fixes every location it matches; promote it to a replacement if it strictly
   supersets a narrower rule. Kills redundancy and rule-set bloat far better than textual novelty.

6. **Run the whole rule set to fixpoint on the corpus with cycle + overlap detection (ESLint/RuboCop).**
   A bounded multi-pass loop with output-hash cycle detection and overlap ("clobbering") skipping;
   treat any new rule that induces a cycle or overlaps an existing rule as a gate failure. Essential
   as the auto-generated set grows.

7. **Close the refine loop over external signals only (Huang et al.).** Intrinsic self-critique
   degrades quality; feed the *actual* corpus over-fires, mutation survivors, and equivalence
   counterexamples back into each agent iteration. Prevents confident-but-wrong self-approval.

8. **Guard tuning by differential testing (SafeRefactor).** Generate many small programs the guard
   accepts, run before/after: behavioral divergence ⇒ guard too weak (over-fire); accepted-but-
   unfixed ⇒ guard too strong (missed generality). An automatic knob for both precision and generality.

9. **Mutate the guard/LHS in the mutation gate, and demand a "repair precondition."** Mutation-test
   the matcher (drop context, loosen arity, flip literal) — surviving guard mutants flag under-tested/
   over-general rules. Pair with Sorald-style "only fire where preconditions guarantee safety; else
   decline." Adopt a concrete precision target (SpongeBugs shipped <0.6% FP for auto-fixes).

10. **Gold benchmark + prompt/model bake-off + memory for the classifier (Semgrep Assistant).**
    Maintain a held-out set of accept/reject rule decisions, evaluate prompts/models against it
    (promptfoo-style), and feed prior decisions + curated positive/negative snippets as context so
    the classifier stops re-proposing near-duplicates and its judgments stay calibrated. Longer-term:
    per-rule revert telemetry with probation/auto-demote (Tricorder's <10% FP trust threshold).
